The ROM was validated against computational predictions from the experimentally validated 2D cross-section model for sulfur TES pilot prototype design (Figure 1). Contrary to the lab prototype unit shown in Figure 20 that was originally designed for integration with combined heat and power system with separate internal charge (for flowing hot exhaust air during charge) and discharge circuits (for flowing thermal oil HTF during discharge), the pilot system used the same circuit for both charge and discharge. In total there are two parallel serpentine circuits, and the configuration is symmetrical about the vertical diametral axis. Figures 39 and 40 show the transient variation in sulfur temperature during charge and discharge, respectively. During charge (Figure 39), hot HTF from solar thermal enters the internal heat exchanger from the top and cold HTF after transferring heat to molten sulfur exits TES from the bottom (to be heated in the solar receiver). During discharge (Figure 40), hot HTF exits from the top to deliver energy for steam generation in a thermal oil to steam/heat exchanger (steam is the typical industrial process heat medium) while cold HTF returning from the heat exchanger enters the internal heat exchange port at the bottom of the vessel. The ROM was further validated using experimental results from pilot prototype in Task 11 and was extensively used for design exploration and technoeconomic analysis due to its quick computational run time. It was observed that the prediction from ROM agrees very well with high fidelity CFD results with an average error < 5%. This also verified the fidelity of the numerical approach to use a 2D unit cell with wall temperature boundary condition to inform the sulfur-side heat transfer coefficient in the ROM. Sulfur TES Performance Evaluation: A transient computational analysis of sulfur TES using the validated ROM was performed for repeated charge and discharge cycles to investigate its dynamic response. An industrial process heat load of 45 MW was considered.
